info.name: csph-gateway
info.description:
# CSPH - API Gateway collection (the realistic path)

Every request goes through the **Spring Cloud Gateway** on `{{gateway}}` (`http://localhost:8080`). This is the path
a browser or mobile client actually takes: JWT in, security headers injected downstream, `@RequiresPermission`
enforced by `PermissionAspect`.

## Run order

```
00 - Health & Discovery      no auth needed (except the second actuator request)
01 - Auth                    <-- LOGIN HERE; everything downstream needs accessToken
01b - Auth negative cases    must 401
02 - Organization Service    captures orgId, marketerOrgId, transporterOrgId, clientOrgId, siteId, siteIdDest
03 - User Service            captures personIdNew, personIdLogin, roleId, groupId, permissionId
04 - Tour Service            captures tourId, checkpointId, pickupId, contractId
05 - Cylinder Service        captures cylinderId, rfidTagId, tagUid, scanEventId
06 - Fleet & IoT Service     captures vehicleId, deviceId
07 - Subsidy Service         captures declarationId, reconciliationId, redressementId
08 - Audit Service
09 - Notification Service    captures templateCode
```

Run the **collection**, not single requests, so the collection-level pre-request script regenerates `uniq` for
each one.

## Response envelope gotcha

Most endpoints answer `{"success":bool,"message":str,"data":...}`. These answer a **bare `PageResponse`** with no
envelope at all:

`/api/v1/organizations`, `/api/v1/sites`, `/api/v1/persons/`, `/api/v1/users/`, `/api/v1/cylinders`,
`/api/v1/rfid`, `/api/v1/scans`

And `/api/v1/telemetry/vehicles/*` answers a bare object / bare array. `PageResponse` serialises `member` as the
primary field plus the `content` and `totalElements` aliases, so the tests here accept either.

Whether a response is enveloped is decided **per method signature, not per service** - organization-service alone
has both, in the same controller.

## Gateway 401 bodies are plain text

`Missing Authorization Header`, `Invalid Authorization Header`, `Invalid JWT Token` - raw bytes, not JSON. Do not
assert a JSON envelope on those.

## Companion

`csph-services-direct` hits each service on its own port with no gateway and no JWT, which is what makes
`PermissionAspect` skip every `@RequiresPermission` check. Use it to explore the endpoint surface; use this
collection to verify what a real client actually sees.

item.description:
Is the whole platform up? Gateway actuator, the Eureka registry, and the aggregated OpenAPI documents the gateway
re-exposes at `/v3/api-docs/<service-id>`.

`/v3/api-docs*` is in `JwtAuthenticationFilter.OPEN_ENDPOINTS`, so none of these need a token.

The two actuator requests are deliberately a pair: the first is the cold-start probe (401 is fine, it proves the
process is alive), the second needs `01 - Auth > Login` to have run and gives a hard 200.

item.name: 01 - Auth

request.description:
`AuthController.login` -> `ApiResponse<LoginResponse>`.

**Seeded logins - 13 users, every one of them password `Password123!`, and `personId == username`:**

| username | org | seeded by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `superadmin.cspHq` | CSPH | `AuthDataInitializer` |
| `admin.cspHq` | CSPH | " |
| `superviseur.cspHq` | CSPH | " |
| `integrateur.cspHq` | CSPH | " |
| `operateur.dla` | DEP-DLA | " |
| `emplisseur.dla` | DEP-DLA | " |
| `operateur.yde` | DEP-YDE | " |
| `gest.gpl` | MKT-GPL | " |
| `agent.gpl` | MKT-GPL | " |
| `chauffeur.abc1` | TRP-ABC | " |
| `chauffeur.abc2` | TRP-ABC | " |
| `resp.abc` | TRP-ABC | " |
| `resp.industries` | CLT-IND | " |

**`ipAddress` and `deviceInfo` are mandatory in practice.** Only `username` / `password` are `@NotBlank`, but
`AuthService.login` writes `request.getIpAddress()` into `auth_users.last_login_ip` and both fields into
`refresh_tokens`. Omit `ipAddress` and the first login stores a short/NULL value that overflows its column on the
*next* login - the classic "worked once, then never again" trap.

### Why the `permissions` test decodes the JWT

`LoginResponse` has **no** `permissions` field. Permissions are resolved at login, baked into the JWT
`permissions` claim, and lifted back out by the gateway into the `X-User-Permissions` header. So the test below
decodes the access token payload. `roles`, on the other hand, *is* serialised - but it is legitimately `[]` when
user-service is unreachable (`AuthService` swallows that error), so that test only rejects raw UUIDs.

Token rotation. `AuthService.refreshToken` marks the presented token `revoked` and issues a fresh pair - so the
old `{{refreshToken}}` is dead once this succeeds. Needs the value captured by the login request, i.e. run it second.

`TokenRefreshResponse` carries **only** `accessToken`, `refreshToken`, `tokenType`, `expiresIn` - no `personId`, no
`roles`. That is why this test does not overwrite `personId`.

`MeController.me` requires `X-User-PersonId`; through the gateway the `JwtAuthenticationFilter` injects it from the
JWT `sub` claim, so it is always present. Sending it by hand is belt-and-braces (and it matters in the direct-port
collection, where there is no gateway).

`roles` here is split straight out of the `X-User-Roles` header the gateway injected, so it mirrors what login returned.

The end-to-end proof that the gateway header pipeline works end to end: auth-service resolves the permissions from
user-service at login, bakes them into the JWT, the gateway lifts them back out into `X-User-Permissions`, and this
endpoint does nothing but split that header on commas.

If this is `[]` while the login JWT claim was non-empty, the `JwtAuthenticationFilter` is not running.

`UpdateMeRequest` accepts only `email`, and it is `@Email` validated - so a malformed address is a 400.

**Side effect, stated plainly:** this really overwrites `auth_users.email` for the logged-in user. The value is
unique per run (`{{uniq}}`) so re-runs never 409, but the seeded `superadmin.cspHq` address stays changed to
whatever ran last. Logins are by username, so nothing else breaks.

**Run this last in the folder, by design.** `AuthService.logout` does `refreshTokenRepository.deleteByPersonId(personId)`
- it wipes *every* refresh token for the person, not just this one.

The access token keeps working until it expires (the gateway never calls back into auth-service), so folders
`02`-`09` are unaffected. But `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` will fail afterwards - re-run `01 - Auth` from the top for
a clean session.

item.description:
**Login is the keystone of the whole suite.** It is the only request that publishes `accessToken`, and every folder
from `02` onwards reads it. Nothing downstream works without running this folder first.

`ipAddress` + `deviceInfo` are not optional decoration - see the request description for the column-overflow trap.

> `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` is deliberately last in this folder: it invalidates all refresh tokens for the person.

item.name: 01b - Auth negative cases

request.description:
`X-User-PersonId` is present but there is no `Authorization` header, so `JwtAuthenticationFilter` short-circuits
before the route is even resolved -> 401 `Missing Authorization Header`.

The downstream service is never reached. That is the point: the gateway is the only authentication boundary in the
platform - which is exactly what the companion `csph-services-direct` collection demonstrates from the other side.

Well-formed `Bearer ` prefix, junk token. The header passes the `startsWith('Bearer ')` check, then
`Jwts.parser().verifyWith(...)` throws and the filter answers 401 `Invalid JWT Token`.

This is also what `Bearer {{accessToken}}` produces while `accessToken` is still empty - i.e. running this folder
before `01 - Auth` lands here too. That is intentional: it means an un-run collection fails with a clear 401 rather
than a confusing 500.

Same guard, different route: `GatewayConfig` attaches the JWT filter to the `organization-service-sites` route
(`/api/v1/sites/**`) as well as to auth-service. Proves the filter is wired per route, not globally once.

item.description:
Three requests that **must** answer 401.

The gateway's `JwtAuthenticationFilter.onError` writes the reason as raw bytes - `Missing Authorization Header`,
`Invalid Authorization Header`, `Invalid JWT Token` - so these bodies are **plain text, not JSON**. Do not assert a
JSON envelope here. (`Authorization: ` with an empty token also yields 401 `Invalid JWT Token`, which is why this
folder passes even on a cold, never-logged-in collection.)

item.name: 02 - Organization Service

request.description:
`OrganizationController.listOrganizations` returns `PageResponse<OrganizationSummaryResponse>` **directly**, not
wrapped in `ApiResponse` - so there is no `success` key. That asymmetry is per-controller, and this is the
canonical example of it.

This request is also the suite's organization bootstrap. It captures:

* `orgId` - row 0's UUID, used by everything else in this folder
* `marketerOrgId`, `transporterOrgId`, `clientOrgId` - needed by folders `04` and `07`

The role matching is deliberately lenient. Depending on which seeder won, `type` holds either the enum **code**
(`MKT` / `TRP` / `CLT`, from `DataInitializer`) or the enum **name** (`MARKETEUR` / `TRANSPORTEUR` / `CLIENT`, from
the Flyway seed), so both spellings are accepted, with a fallback to `orgId` so even a sparse database produces a
runnable suite.

Single organization, **enveloped** (`ApiResponse<OrganizationResponse>`) - the opposite of the list request directly
above, same controller, same service. Worth internalising: envelope-vs-bare is decided per method signature, not
per service.

`{orgId}` is the UUID primary key, not the business `code` (`CSPH`, `MKT-GPL`, `TRP-ABC`, `CLT-IND`, `DEP-DLA`,
`DEP-YDE` - the latter two come from the org seeder rather than the Flyway seed).

`CreateOrganizationRequest` requires `code`, `name`, `type`, `tier` (all `@NotBlank`). `Organization.code` is
`UNIQUE`, so a fixed literal 409s on the second run - the code is `TST-{{uniq}}`, regenerated per request by the
collection pre-request script. That single change is what makes the whole collection re-runnable.

`type` is the `OrganizationType` code (`REG`, `DEP`, `MKT`, `TRP`, `CLT`, `INT`, `PLT`); `tier` is the
`OrganizationTier` name (`TIER_1_GOVERNANCE` ... `TIER_4_CONSUMPTION`). Both columns are free-form strings.

`X-User-PersonId` is a **required** `@RequestHeader` on this method (no `required = false`), so omitting it is a
400 from `MissingRequestHeaderException` - not a 403 from the permission aspect. That distinction matters when
triaging failures: a 400 here is a malformed request, a 403 is a missing permission.

This request **overwrites** `orgId`, so the requests after it operate on the throwaway org and the `DELETE` at the
end of the folder cleans up after them.

{
  "code": "TST-{{uniq}}",
  "name": "Postman Test Org {{uniq}}",
  "description": "Created by the csph-gateway Postman collection",
  "type": "MKT",
  "tier": "T3",
  "contactEmail": "pm-{{uniq}}@cspHq.cm",
  "contactPhone": "+237699000000",
  "website": "https://csph.cm/{{uniq}}",
  "isHeadquarters": false
}

request.description:
`UpdateOrganizationRequest` has **no** `code` field and **no** `@NotBlank` anywhere - it is a partial update of
descriptive fields only. Sending `code` would be silently ignored, which is why the unique-code strategy does not
need repeating here. An empty JSON body is a legal request against this endpoint.

{
  "name": "Postman Test Org {{uniq}} (updated)",
  "description": "Updated by the csph-gateway Postman collection",
  "contactPhone": "+237699111111",
  "website": "https://csph.cm/{{uniq}}/updated",
  "currency": "XAF",
  "language": "FR",
  "timezone": "Africa/Douala"
}

request.description:
`UpdateStatusRequest` = `{newStatus, reason}` - the platform-wide status-lifecycle shape; the identical class name
appears in organization-service, user-service and elsewhere with a matching contract.

`OrganizationService.updateStatus` is a plain `org.setStatus(...)` with **no enum validation**, so any string is
accepted. `INACTIVE` is used here deliberately: it is a real `EntityStatus` value that does not gate any of the
reads that follow. (Compare the site request below, whose value does come from a closed enum.)

Direct children in the organization tree. Enveloped **array** (`ApiResponse<List<OrganizationSummaryResponse>>`),
not a paged object - three shapes in one controller: bare page, enveloped object, enveloped array.

On the throwaway org created two requests ago this is legitimately `[]`. The assertion accepts an empty array; a
non-array would mean the endpoint changed shape.

Declared as `ApiResponse<Object>` because the payload is a recursive tree - an object at one depth, an array at
another. Asserted defensively (defined and not null) rather than typed, which is the honest thing to do for an
`Object` return.

Like `/organizations`, this returns a **bare** `PageResponse` - no `success` envelope.

Captures `siteId` (row 0) and `siteIdDest` (row 1, falling back to `siteId`). Both are consumed downstream: `siteId`
by the person-site assignment in folder `03` and by the checkpoint in folder `04`; `siteIdDest` as the pickup
destination in folder `04`.

**`siteId` here is the primary key, not the business key.** Seeded business keys are `SITE-CSPH-HQ`,
`SITE-DEP-DLA-PRINCIPAL`, `SITE-DEP-DLA-FIL`, `SITE-DEP-YDE-PRINCIPAL`, `SITE-MKT-GPL-ENTREPOT`,
`SITE-TRP-ABC-DEPOT`, `SITE-CLT-IND-RECEPTION` (exposed as the `siteCode*` environment variables). The
`{id}` path variable wants the UUID.

Single site, enveloped (`ApiResponse<SiteResponse>`).

Note that `SiteResponse` exposes **both** `id` (primary key) and `siteId` (business key) - that field-name collision
is why the path variables across this collection look inconsistent until you know to expect it.

Geo query around Douala (3.848 N, 11.502 E) within 50 km - the CSPH operating area.

All three parameters are **required** and declared as primitive `double`, not boxed `Double`, so a missing one is a
400 `MissingServletRequestParameterException` rather than a null that gets filtered out.

Enveloped **array** (`ApiResponse<List<SiteSummaryResponse>>`). An empty result within 50 km of Douala just means
no depot has been geocoded yet - not a failure.

`CreateSiteRequest` requires `code`, `siteId`, `name`, `organizationId`, `type` (all `@NotBlank`).

**Two** unique constraints apply, hence `{{uniq}}` in both `code` and `name`: `Site.code` is `UNIQUE`, and
`(organizationId, name)` is `UNIQUE`. Forgetting the second one is what produces an intermittent 409 on re-runs.

`type` is the `SiteType` code: `DEP` depot, `FIL` filling centre, `WHS` warehouse, `OFC` office, `CST` client site,
`TRP` transit point.

Overwrites `siteId` with the new primary key, so the client-site request below targets a site that is guaranteed not
to have a client-site row yet.

{
  "code": "SITE-{{uniq}}",
  "siteId": "SI-{{uniq}}",
  "name": "Postman Depot {{uniq}}",
  "description": "Created by the csph-gateway Postman collection",
  "organizationId": "{{orgId}}",
  "type": "DEP",
  "addressLine1": "Rue de la Joie",
  "city": "Douala",
  "region": "Littoral",
  "latitude": 4.0511,
  "longitude": 9.7679,
  "geofenceRadiusMeters": 300,
  "storageCapacityTons": 500.0,
  "maxVehicleBays": 12
}

request.description:
Same `{newStatus, reason}` contract as the organization call, but the site status column is a **closed enum**:
`UNASSIGNED`, `ASSIGNED`, `ACTIVE`, `VERIFIED`, `SUSPENDED`, `REJECTED` (`SiteStatusEnum`). An unrecognised value
would fail at the database rather than at a bean validation, which is a worse failure mode - so the value is drawn
from the enum.

Client sites - a site bound to a CLIENT organization (filling centre, reseller, industrial consumer). This is the
`client_sites` join table that the tour service's checkpoints reference as `clientSiteId`.

This one is **enveloped** `ApiResponse<PageResponse<ClientSiteResponse>>`, the opposite of `/sites` two requests up -
same service, different controller, different convention. That is why the suite asserts per-endpoint rather than
per-service.

`CreateClientSiteRequest` requires `siteId` + `clientOrganizationId`.

`siteId` is the **site primary key** (`client_sites.site_id UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE`), not the business key. A site can
be a client site **at most once, ever** - and that unique constraint is the reason this test tolerates 409 instead
of demanding a 2xx. No per-run trick can make it unique, because the constraint is on the site, not on a free-text
column.

On a clean run the site was created two requests ago, so you get 200. Re-run against a database where that site is
already a client site and you get 409 - correct behaviour, not a failure. Both `DuplicateResourceException` and
`DataIntegrityViolationException` map to 409 in `GlobalExceptionHandler`.

body.raw:
{
  "siteId": "{{siteId}}",
  "clientOrganizationId": "{{clientOrgId}}",
  "siteContactPersonId": "{{personId}}",
  "deliveryInstructions": "Call 30 minutes before arrival - Postman probe",
  "specificRequirements": "Cylinder swap only",
  "requiresAuthorization": true,
  "operatingConstraints": "Weekdays 08:00-17:00"
}

request.description:
Reverse lookup: given a site, return its client-site binding. A **single** enveloped object, not a list.

**404 is the normal case** for a freshly created operational depot - only sites typed `CST` / bound to a CLIENT org
carry a client-site row. The assertion accepts both, and on 200 it cross-checks that the returned `siteId` is the
one we asked about.

The class-structure taxonomy (`class_structures`) used to classify organizations.

Read-only - `ClassStructureController` declares a single `GET`, no POST/PUT. It is reference data, which is why
there is no create step for it anywhere in this suite.

Directed org-to-org link. `type` must be a `RelationshipType` code: `MANDATE`, `CONTRACT`, `SUPPLY`, `SUBSIDIARY`,
`FRANCHISE`, `SUPERVISION`. `SUPPLY` is the depot -> marketer supply link.

`OrganizationRelationshipController` is **POST-only** - no GET exists, so this response is the only way to see what
you created. There is no unique constraint on the `(source, target)` pair, so re-runs append rows rather than
409ing; that is correct for what is effectively an append-only relationship log, and `contractReference` carries
`{{uniq}}` so the rows are still distinguishable.

body.raw:
{
  "sourceOrganizationId": "{{orgId}}",
  "targetOrganizationId": "{{marketerOrgId}}",
  "type": "SUPPLY",
  "contractReference": "PM-{{uniq}}",
  "validFrom": "{{periodStart}}",
  "validUntil": "{{periodEnd}}",
  "isExclusive": false,
  "description": "Created by the csph-gateway Postman collection"
}

request.description:
**Last request in folder `02` on purpose** - it archives the throwaway organization created earlier in the folder.

`OrganizationService.deleteOrganization` is a **soft delete**: it only does `org.setStatus("ARCHIVED")`. The row
survives, which is exactly why the `{{uniq}}` codes still matter for re-runnability, and why the collection leaves
archived `TST-PM...` rows behind after every run.

item.description:
organization-service on :8082, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1`.

**Captures:** `orgId`, `marketerOrgId`, `transporterOrgId`, `clientOrgId` (folders `04` and `07` need them),
`siteId` + `siteIdDest` (folders `03`, `04`, `05` need them), `clientSiteId`.

**Bare vs envelope, both in this folder:** `GET /organizations` and `GET /sites` return a **bare `PageResponse`**;
`GET /organizations/{id}`, `/children`, `/hierarchy`, `/sites/{id}`, `/sites/nearby`, `/client-sites`,
`/client-sites/by-site/{id}`, `/classifications` are all enveloped. The distinction is a property of each method's
return type, not of the service - and it is the single most common cause of a Postman test that "should" pass.

item.name: 03 - User Service
GET /roles/  (BOOTSTRAP roleId for the assign-role step)

request.description:
Bootstrap request, deliberately placed first in this folder.

`POST /persons/{id}/roles` needs a `roleId`, but `POST /roles/` runs twelve requests later - so without this
bootstrap the assignment step would send an empty `roleId` and fail `@NotBlank` validation. It captures the first
existing role (normally `SUPERADMIN`) as a usable `roleId`. `POST /roles/` later overwrites it with the role it
creates, which is what the three requests after that one use.

Enveloped **array** (`ApiResponse<List<RoleResponse>>`), **not** a paged object. The trailing slash is required.

**The trailing slash is required.** `PersonController` is mapped
`@RequestMapping({"/api/v1/persons", "/api/v1/users"})` with `@GetMapping("/")` - `/api/v1/persons` without the slash
is a plain 404, not a redirect.

Returns a **bare** `PageResponse<PersonSummaryResponse>` - no `success` envelope.

### Two identifiers, one name

This request resolves the logged-in user deterministically: it looks for the row whose **`personId`** equals the
`personId` variable (a *business* key, `superadmin.cspHq`) and stores that row's **`id`** (a UUID) into
`personIdNew` - because every `/persons/{id}/...` path variable in this folder expects the UUID. It also publishes
the business key as `personIdLogin`.

They are separate columns. `AuthDataInitializer` happens to seed them equal (`personId = username`), which is why
the distinction is easy to miss until a request 404s.

`PersonController` is mapped to **both** `/api/v1/persons` and `/api/v1/users` for frontend compatibility, so this
is literally the same handler behind a second path. The frontend historically called `/users`, which is why the
alias exists. Use `/persons/` for anything new.

Same bare `PageResponse`, same trailing-slash requirement.

`{id}` is the **UUID primary key**, not the business key. Passing `superadmin.cspHq` here 404s - use
`/persons/by-person-id/{businessKey}` for that. The pairing of those two routes is the most common 404 in this API.

Enveloped `ApiResponse<PersonResponse>` - the richest person payload available: names, contact details, address,
org/site scope, avatar, plus the nested `phones` / `emails` collections that the dedicated sub-resources return.

The business-key lookup, e.g. `/persons/by-person-id/superadmin.cspHq`.

This is the endpoint `AuthService` calls during login to resolve the caller's roles, and it carries **no**
`@RequiresPermission` - which is why it answers even from contexts where the other person routes would 403.

Order of the path segments is what distinguishes the two lookups: `by-person-id/{key}` vs `{uuid}`.

`CreatePersonRequest` requires only `firstName` + `lastName`. The nested `phones` / `emails` arrays are optional and
are exactly what the `/phones` and `/emails` sub-resources return afterwards - the assertions two requests down
verify that round-trip rather than just the shape.

`email` carries `{{uniq}}` so repeated runs do not collide on the unique-email constraint.

Returns **200, not 201** - the handler returns `ApiResponse` directly rather than through a `ResponseEntity`, so
Spring's default 200 applies. There is also a sibling `POST /persons/with-auth` that additionally provisions
auth-service credentials, which is what a driver account needs.

There is **no** `DELETE /persons/{id}`: persons are never deleted through this API.

Overwrites `personIdNew` (the new UUID) and `personIdLogin` (its business key) for the rest of the folder.

Partial update of profile fields. `UpdatePersonRequest` carries no `@NotBlank`, so an empty body is legal - the only
thing this endpoint truly requires is the person id in the path.

`deviceClass` + `deviceClassDescription` are the GPL-specific fields deciding which mobile app (Pocket PC / PDA) a
person is licensed for; `wfMailElection` and `transEmailElection` are the per-person opt-in flags for the workflow
and transport notification mails. Those flags are why a notification to a seeded operator may be a no-op.

request.description:
The same `{newStatus, reason}` status-lifecycle body as organizations and sites - `UpdateStatusRequest` is duplicated
across three modules with an identical contract, and the `PATCH /{id}/status` route shape is the platform convention.

The person was created in this same run, so marking it `INACTIVE` breaks nothing downstream.

Phone sub-resource, projected server-side (`personService.getPerson(id).getPhones()`). Enveloped **array**.

Returns the `phones` array sent in the `POST /persons/` body a few requests up, so the assertion checks the
round-trip rather than only the shape.

Email sub-resource - the counterpart of `/phones`. Enveloped **array**.

Email matters well beyond the UI: notification-service resolves a recipient through `recipientPersonId`, and any
`EMAIL`-channel send needs a resolvable address. A person with no `emails` row cannot be notified at all.

Role assignments, queried by the person''s **business** `personId` - the controller resolves
`personService.getPerson(id).getPersonId()` before delegating, so the UUID in the path is only used for the lookup.

Returns `UserRoleAssignment` entities, each with a validity window (`validFrom` / `validUntil`) and an `isPrimary`
flag - which is how one person holds several roles with different scopes at once.

`AssignRoleRequest` requires `personId` **and** `roleId` (`@NotBlank`), and `personId` is the **business key** -
even though the controller overwrites it with the value it resolves. `@Valid` runs at binding time, *before* the
controller body, so leaving `personId` out of the JSON is a 400 even though the server would have filled it in.

`roleId` comes from the bootstrap `GET /roles/` at the top of this folder. `siteId` scopes the grant to a single
site; omit it for an organisation-wide grant.

Site assignments (`UserSiteAssignment`) - the second half of the dual-layer RBAC: a person gets **roles** (what they
may do) and **sites** (where they may do it). Data-visibility filtering is built on the site assignments, not on
the roles, so a person with roles but no sites is functionally blind.

Empty before the POST below, which uses the `siteId` captured in folder `02`.

`AssignSiteRequest` requires `personId` + `siteId`, for the same validation-timing reason as the role assignment.
`isPrimary` / `isDefault` pick the person's home site, which the frontend uses as the default filter.

This is the request that makes a person visible in site-scoped listings - without it they exist but can see nothing.

The **effective** permission set for the person, flattened from every granted role by
`PermissionService.resolvePermissions(personId)`.

This is the exact call `AuthService` makes at login to build the JWT `permissions` claim - so running it on any
person tells you exactly what that person's next login token will contain, without having to log in as them.

A `Set<String>` serialises as a JSON **array**, hence the array assertion (and not a `PageResponse`).

The full role list. Despite looking like the paged `/persons/` and `/organizations/` endpoints, this one is
`ApiResponse<List<RoleResponse>>` - an **enveloped array, not a `PageResponse`**. Same for `/groups/` and
`/permissions/`.

Trailing slash required (`@GetMapping("/")`).

`CreateRoleRequest` requires `code` + `name`, and `Role.code` is `UNIQUE` - hence `{{uniq}}`.

**These roles live in the `roles` table (JPA `Role` entity), not the seeded `system_roles` enum table.** That is why
an arbitrary code like `ROLE-PM...` is accepted here even though the 8 seeded `system_role` names (SUPERADMIN, ADMIN,
SUPERVISOR, INTEGRATEUR, AGENT, MARKETEUR, TRANSPORTEUR, LIVREUR) are a closed Postgres enum on the *other* table.
Two role concepts, one API surface - worth knowing before you try to create a role named `SUPERADMIN`.

Overwrites `roleId`, so the three requests after this one operate on the new role.

request.description:
Single role. `RoleResponse` nests its granted `permissions` inline, so this one call shows the role's full permission
set without a second round-trip.

Only the permissions whose grant row has `granted = true` - `RoleService.getPermissionsForRole` filters on that
flag, so a revoked-but-still-stored row is invisible here. Enveloped **array**.

Legitimately empty on the role just created; the next request fills it.

**`permissionId` is a required query parameter and this endpoint takes no request body at all.**
`grantPermission(id, @RequestParam String permissionId, ...)` - putting it in a JSON body is the single most common
mistake here, and it fails with a 400 that gives no hint about the real cause.

`{{permissionId}}` comes from `GET /permissions/` below. On a cold, never-run collection it is empty, so this
request 400s until that request has been sent once - the folder order already accounts for it, and the test
distinguishes the two cases instead of failing blindly.

Re-granting a permission a role already holds is harmless, so re-runs are safe. The counterpart
`DELETE /roles/{roleId}/permissions/{permissionId}` exists but is not exercised here.

item.name: GET /permissions/  (TRAILING SLASH - catalog, also captures permissionId)

request.description:
The whole permission catalog, straight from `repository.findAll()`. Enveloped **array**, trailing slash required.

This is the authoritative list of the `code` strings that every `@RequiresPermission` in the platform checks
against, and the source of `{{permissionId}}` for the grant request above.

Note the two coexisting naming styles: organization / user / tour / fleet services use UPPER_SNAKE codes
(`ORG_VIEW`, `SITE_CREATE`, `TOUR_START`, `CHECKPOINT_SKIP`, `fleet.vehicles.read`), while older core modules use
dotted lower-case (`tours.create`). Both styles are live in the same `permissions` table.

Distinct `module` values across the catalog - the grouping the settings and role-editor UI renders as sections.

Route specificity keeps this from colliding with `GET /permissions/{id}`: Spring prefers the literal `/modules`
over the `{id}` template, so a permission whose id happened to be the string `modules` would be unreachable. Not a
practical concern with UUIDs, but it is why the more specific route is declared at all.

User groups - permission bundles used for a bulk grant instead of per-person role assignment. Enveloped **array**,
trailing slash required.

`GroupResponse.memberCount` is maintained denormalised on the row, so this list is the cheapest way to see group
sizes without an N+1 storm of member calls.

`CreateGroupRequest` requires `code`, `name`, `organizationId`. `user_groups.code` is `UNIQUE` (100 chars), so
`{{uniq}}` keeps the folder re-runnable. `siteId` is optional and scopes the group to one site.

`isSystemGroup` is deliberately **not** settable from the API - system groups are the ones the seeder owns and
should not be editable through a REST call.

  "code": "GRP-{{uniq}}",
  "name": "Postman Group {{uniq}}",
  "description": "Created by the csph-gateway Postman collection",
  "organizationId": "{{orgId}}",
  "siteId": "{{siteId}}"
}

request.description:
Single group, enveloped. `memberCount` should read 0 right after creation - the assertion below pins the id, and the
next request shows the roster growing.

Group roster, joined out of `user_group_memberships`. Enveloped **array** of `GroupMemberResponse` (person UUID plus
display name).

Empty until the POST below.

`AddGroupMemberRequest` takes a single `personId` - the **business key** here. (The role and site assignments above
also take business keys but are addressed by UUID in the path; this one has no path id to disambiguate.)

Returns `ApiResponse<Void>`, so `data` is `null` on success - the assertion checks `success`, not `data`. The
counterpart `DELETE /groups/{groupId}/members/{personId}` also takes the business key.

item.description:
user-service on :8083, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1`.

**The trailing slash is mandatory** on `GET /persons/`, `/users/`, `/roles/`, `/groups/`, `/permissions/` - those
controllers are mapped `@GetMapping("/")`. Without the slash: a 404, not a redirect. With the slash: correct.

**Capture order matters inside this folder.** `POST /persons/{id}/roles` needs a `roleId` before `POST /roles/`
runs, so the folder opens with a bootstrap `GET /roles/`; `POST /roles/` then overwrites `roleId` with the role it
creates, which is what the three requests after it use.

**Response shapes are not uniform here:** `GET /persons/` is a **bare** `PageResponse`, while `/roles/`, `/groups/`
and `/permissions/` are **enveloped arrays** (not paged).

item.name: 04 - Tour Service

request.description:
Bootstrap request, deliberately first in this folder.

`POST /tours/{id}/assign-vehicle` declares `@RequestParam String vehicleId` - **required, and it must be in the query
string**. Vehicles are only created in folder `06`, which runs *after* this one, so without this bootstrap the
assignment step would send an empty parameter and 400. Fetching an existing vehicle here is the alternative to
reordering the folders, and it keeps the folder independently runnable.

Note this list is **enveloped** `ApiResponse<PageResponse<VehicleResponse>>` - the opposite of folder `05`'s bare
`PageResponse` lists, in a different service, so nothing would let you guess it.

Delivery tours (`delivery_tours` in the schema, `TourResponseDto` on the wire). Enveloped `PageResponse`.

`TourResponseDto` nests its `checkpoints` inline, so this list alone can show the full itinerary shape - although
the dedicated `/tours/{id}/checkpoints` route below is the cheaper way to fetch one tour's stops.

Statuses follow `PickupStatus`-like ordering: `DRAFT` -> assigned -> started -> closed. Every transition below
respects that.

`CreateTourDto` requires `tourCode`, `marketerOrganizationId`, `executionMode`, `type`, and `requestedQuantity`
(`@NotNull @Positive` - zero or negative is a 400). `tourCode` carries `{{uniq}}` for re-runnability.

* `executionMode` - `INTERNAL` or `EXTERNAL` (`TourExecutionMode`). `INTERNAL` adds a database constraint that a
  transporter must be assigned, so `EXTERNAL` is used here.
* `type` - the load being carried; `VRAC` is the bulk tanker variant (`VehicleTypeEnum` also has
  `BOUTEILLES50KG`).
* `marketerOrganizationId` / `transporterOrganizationId` - captured by the org bootstrap in folder `02`.

Overwrites `tourId`; the last request in this folder deletes it.

Single tour, enveloped. Compare `status` / `statusDate` before and after the `start` and `close` calls further down
the folder - that pair is the cheapest way to see the tour lifecycle actually move.

`UpdateTourDto` mirrors `CreateTourDto` minus the `@NotNull @Positive` constraint on `requestedQuantity`, so a partial
body is accepted. Note the collection pre-request regenerates `{{uniq}}` per request, so the `tourCode` sent here is
*not* the one the create used - which is fine, because `tourCode` is being re-stamped rather than matched. If you
need a stable value across a chain, set it in a pre-request script instead of relying on `{{uniq}}`.

Both query parameters are **optional** here (`@RequestParam(required = false)`) - unlike `assign-vehicle`, whose
`vehicleId` is mandatory. Passing neither is accepted and simply leaves the tour unassigned.

`driverPersonId` is the business key of the driver, whereas `driverId` is a users-table id - they are different
identifiers for the same human, and the platform uses `driverPersonId` for the GPL person linkage. This matters when
folders `05` and `07` filter scan events by `driverPersonId`.

**`vehicleId` is a REQUIRED query parameter** (`@RequestParam String vehicleId`, no `required = false`) and this
endpoint takes no body. Omitting it is a 400 `MissingServletRequestParameterException` - the single most common
failure on this route.

`{{vehicleId}}` was bootstrapped by the `GET /vehicles` request at the top of this folder. If the fleet database is
empty, run folder `06` first to create one.

This is also the request that records `assignedByTransporterPersonId` and `transporterAssignedAt` - the audit trail
of who released which truck.

Lifecycle transition `DRAFT -> IN_PROGRESS` (the tour service reuses the `PickupStatus` vocabulary). `startedAt` is
stamped server-side.

Starting a tour twice is a state-machine error, so this request sits between the assignment steps and the
checkpoint steps - running the folder top to bottom keeps it in a legal state.

The itinerary: an ordered list of stops. Enveloped **array** (not paged - an itinerary is naturally small).

`CheckpointResponseDto` carries `siteId` / `clientSiteId` (mutually exclusive - the schema enforces exactly one),
`sequence`, planned vs actual arrival, and a stop `status` from `StopStatus` (`PENDING`, `REACHED`,
`IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETED`, `SKIPPED`, `DELIVERED`, `PARTIAL`, `REJECTED`).

Two database constraints shape this body:

* `chk_checkpoint_exclusive` - exactly one of `siteId` / `clientSiteId` must be set. Sending both, or neither, is
  rejected by the service.
* `UNIQUE (tournee_id, sequence)` â€” one stop per position per tour. Since the tour is created fresh in this run,
  `sequence: 1` is always free.

`sequence` is `@Min(1)`, and `tourId` is injected from the path, so it must **not** appear in the body.

Overwrites `checkpointId`, which folder `05` reuses as the `checkpointId` on a scan event.

Single stop, enveloped. Note the route shape: checkpoints are addressed **flat** (`/api/v1/checkpoints/{id}`) for
single-stop operations, and **nested** (`/api/v1/tours/{tourId}/checkpoints`) for listing and creation. Both exist in
`CheckpointController`.

Partial update of a stop: resequencing, re-planning the arrival, or stamping a status directly.

Passing `status` here bypasses the `validate` / `skip` actions two requests below - it is the administrative
override, useful for back-office correction and a shortcut past the state machine. This suite uses it to move the
stop forward so the `validate` step has something to act on.

Marks the stop as reached / delivered. Takes no body and no parameters - the driver''s PDA hits exactly this route on
arrival.

Penalised by the reconciliation engine if the actual quantity delivered is short, which is what the declaration
workflow in folder `07` eventually measures.

**`reason` is a REQUIRED query parameter** (`@RequestParam String reason`, no `required = false`) and this endpoint
takes no body. A missing reason is a 400.

Runs after `validate` in the folder, so the stop is already validated and skipping it will legitimately be rejected
by the state machine - the test tolerates 409/422 and logs the reason instead of pretending it is a defect. Skipping
a validated stop is exactly the sort of thing the reconciliation report is designed to surface.

Closes the tour and freezes the two quantities the whole subsidy chain depends on: what left the depot and what
actually arrived. Both are optional query parameters; when omitted they stay null.

Loaded 12 / delivered 11 is deliberate - the 1-unit shortfall is the gap `POST /declarations` and the
reconciliation in folder `07` exist to account for. A short delivery is normal operating data, not an error.

Requires every stop to be resolved, so it sits after the validate/skip steps.

Pickup requests - the demand side of a tour, raised by a marketer for stock at a depot. Enveloped `PageResponse`,
filterable by `marketerOrganizationId`, `sourceSiteId` and `status`.

Lifecycle: `DRAFT -> VALIDATED -> INPROGRESS -> COMPLETED` (or `CANCELLED`). The `approve` / `reject` pair below is
how a CSPH agent validates demand; approval needs the approved quantity, which is a **required** query parameter.

`CreatePickupRequestDto` requires `marketerOrganizationId`, `sourceSiteId` and `destinationSiteId`; `requestedQuantity`
is `@Min(1)`. The two site ids are the depot leaving and the site arriving - the physical twin of a tour.

All three ids were captured in folder `02`. `siteIdDest` falls back to `siteId` when the database has only one site,
so this request still succeeds on a minimal install.

**`approvedQuantity` is a REQUIRED query parameter** and is a primitive `double` - omitting it 400s, and so does
sending a non-numeric value.

11 is deliberately one short of the 12 requested: CSPH agents routinely authorise less than a marketer asks for,
and the difference is the audit trail that the subsidy workflow later reconciles.

Rejects the request. No body, **no parameters at all** - a bare PATCH, so it is trivially easy to call.

Runs after `approve` in the folder, so the pickup is already validated and rejection is correctly refused by the
state machine. That refusal is the assertion here: it proves the lifecycle is actually enforced rather than
accepting any transition.

Transporter contracts - the standing commercial agreement between a marketer and a transporter, as opposed to the
one-off `pickup`. Enveloped `PageResponse`, filterable both ways.

The contract is what makes a tour lawful: a marketer cannot dispatch to a transporter it has no contract with.

`CreateTransporterContractDto` requires the two organisation ids and a `contractReference`. `contractReference`
carries `{{uniq}}` so re-runs do not collide.

`isPrimary` marks this as the marketer''s default transporter - at most one primary per marketer in practice, so
repeated creation of primaries is a data-quality issue even when the API accepts it.

Contracts grouped by marketer - a convenience route returning `ApiResponse<List<...>>` (a plain array, not a
`PageResponse`), for the "who can this marketer dispatch with?" panel in the frontend.

Note the route ordering: `/{id}` would happily swallow `by-marketer` if it were declared first and Spring resolved
greedily, so the literal segment is declared ahead of the `{id}` template in the controller.

Terminates the contract - a business state change, not a delete. The row survives with an end date; tours already
dispatched under it are unaffected, and future dispatch is blocked.

No body, no parameters.

**Last request in folder `04`**, so every state transition above has been exercised before the tour is removed.
Like the organization delete, the tour delete is a **soft delete** (`deleted_at` is a column on `delivery_tours`),
so re-runs do not collide on `tourCode` either way - the `{{uniq}}` code is belt and braces.

item.description:
tour-service on :8086, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1` - delivery tours (`/tours`), their stops
(`/checkpoints`), the demand side (`/pickups`) and transporter contracts (`/contracts`).

**One bootstrap request opens the folder.** `assign-vehicle` requires `vehicleId` in the query string, but vehicles
are created in folder `06`, which runs later - so an existing vehicle is fetched here instead. That keeps folder
`04` runnable on its own rather than depending on a folder below it.

**The lifecycle order is real:** create -> assign-driver -> assign-vehicle -> start -> checkpoints ->
validate/skip -> close -> delete. Steps after a state transition can legitimately 409/422, and those assertions
tolerate it and log the body rather than pretending a rejection is a defect.

item.name: 05 - Cylinder Service

request.description:
Bottles. Filterable by `ownerOrganizationId`, `currentSiteId`, `brand`, `capacityKg` and `status`, and always sorted
`createdAt DESC`.

**Bare `PageResponse`**, no `success` envelope - the third service (after organization and user) to use that shape
for its list route. The tests are written per endpoint precisely because there is no per-service rule.

`CreateCylinderRequest` requires only `serialNumber` (`@NotBlank`); the ownership and location fields are what make
it useful, so they are filled from the ids folder `02` captured.

`serialNumber` carries `{{uniq}}` because it is the bottle's identity in the field and collisions there are real
world events, not test artefacts.

`fillStatus` (`EMPTY` / `FULL` / ...) and `status` are independent axes: a bottle can be physically full and
administratively blocked.

Single bottle, enveloped. `CylinderResponse` is the join of the physical asset (serial, brand, capacity) and its
administrative state (holder, site, fill status) - which is why "where is this bottle" and "is this bottle usable"
are the same record.

Full-width update (`UpdateCylinderRequest` mirrors the create DTO). `capacityKg` and `cylinderTypeId` are changed
together here on purpose: in the GPL domain a bottle''s type and its capacity must agree, and mutating one without
the other is the kind of inconsistency that surfaces weeks later in a subsidy audit.

**`targetSiteId` is a REQUIRED body field** (`@NotBlank`) - this one is in the JSON, unlike the tour service''s
`assign-vehicle`, which wants a query parameter. Two different conventions for "required target" in the same
codebase; the request body is the more common one.

A transfer is a custody change, not a movement log entry: it rewrites `currentHolderOrganizationId` and
`currentSiteId` and should emit an audit event. `notes` is free text and is what a supervisor reads afterwards.

RFID tags. **Bare `PageResponse`**, filterable by `tagUid`, `bottleSerial`, `currentSiteId`, `status`, sorted
`createdAt DESC`.

A tag is the physical identity; a bottle is the asset. `rfid_tags.current_site_id` and `current_client_site_id` are
mutually exclusive by a check constraint - a tag is either at an operational site or at a client site, never both.
That same constraint is why the checkpoint body in folder `04` must pick one field and not both.

`status` follows `RfidTagStatus`: `AVAILABLE`, `ASSIGNEDTOBOTTLE`, `INTRANSITOUT`, `INTRANSITIN`, `LOST`, `BLOCKED`.

`CreateRfidTagRequest` requires only `tagUid` (`@NotBlank`) - the EPC identifier written into the tag''s memory.

**`bottleSerial` has a database CHECK constraint: `^[A-Z0-9]{8,}$`.** Uppercase alphanumeric only, at least 8
characters, no dashes. The body uses `BT` + a 15-character timestamp, so it satisfies the constraint; a value like
`BT-2026-01` would be rejected by Postgres rather than by bean validation, which is a much worse error to debug.
`tagUid` deliberately has no such constraint.

Captures both identifiers: `rfidTagId` (the UUID, for the `/rfid/{id}` routes) and `tagUid` (the EPC, for
`/rfid/tag/{tagUid}`) - they are different columns and both are needed below.

By **primary key**. Compare the `/rfid/tag/{tagUid}` route below, which is the same resource addressed by its EPC -
the same two-identifier pattern as `persons/{id}` vs `persons/by-person-id/{key}` in folder `03`.

By **EPC / tag UID** - which is how the handheld reader addresses a tag: it reads the EPC and asks "what is this?",
never "what is the id of the row whose id I already know".

`{{tagUid}}` was captured by the `POST /rfid` request above. It is empty on a cold run, in which case the path
degenerates to `/rfid/tag/` and 404s - tolerated by the test.

Updates the tag''s state. Moving to `ASSIGNEDTOBOTTLE` while `currentSiteId` is still an operational site is exactly
the mixed state the reconciliation report exists to catch: the tag claims a bottle but the bottle is not in
transit.

`bottleSerial` again obeys the `^[A-Z0-9]{8,}$` check constraint.

body.raw:
{
  "tagUid": "{{tagUid}}",
  "bottleSerial": "BT{{uniq}}",
  "currentSiteId": "{{siteId}}",
  "status": "ASSIGNEDTOBOTTLE",
  "statusDescription": "Paired with a bottle by the csph-gateway Postman collection"
}

request.description:
Scan events - one row per tag read at a checkpoint, and the raw material of every reconciliation in folder `07`.
**Bare `PageResponse`**, filterable by `checkpointId`, `driverPersonId`, `rfidTagId`, `direction`, sorted
`timestamp DESC`.

`direction` is `IN` or `OUT` (`ScanDirection`). A physically impossible sequence - two `OUT`s without an `IN` - is
what sets `conflictStatus` and creates the work the `resolve-conflict` route below exists to clear.

`CreateScanEventRequest` requires only `rfidTagId` (`@NotBlank`); the rest is the evidence bundle that makes a scan
admissible later.

`checkpointId` and `rfidTagId` come from folders `04` and `05` respectively, and `scan_events.checkpoint_id` is
`NOT NULL` in the schema - so **folder `04` must have run** for this request to succeed. This is the one hard
ordering dependency left in the suite, and the folder description calls it out.

`pdaSyncId` is the handheld''s client-side id: it makes ingestion idempotent when a PDA reconnects after a signal
blackspot and replays its buffer, which is the normal case in the field.

Single scan, enveloped. `conflictStatus` is the field to read here: a non-null value means the event needs manual
adjudication, which is precisely what the next request performs.

Manual adjudication of a conflicting scan. `resolutionAction` is a **required body field** (`@NotBlank`); `notes` is
the audit justification and should always be filled in a real investigation.

A scan that is not in conflict will normally be rejected here by the state machine - the test tolerates that and
logs it, because "no conflict to resolve" is a correct answer, not a failure.

**Last request in folder `05`**, cleaning up the bottle created near the top. The RFID tag created in this folder is
deliberately **not** deleted - a tag outlives the bottles it has been paired with, and the audit trail of a retired
tag matters.

As with the organization delete, this is a soft delete (the entity carries `deleted_at`), so the row survives and
`{{uniq}}` in the serial keeps re-runs collision-free regardless.

item.description:
cylinder-service on :8087, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1` - the physical layer: bottles (`/cylinders`), the
RFID tags that identify them (`/rfid`) and the scan events that prove custody moved (`/scans`).

**All three list routes here are bare `PageResponse`** - no `success` envelope, unlike everything else in this
folder.

**One hard ordering dependency:** `POST /scans` needs a `checkpointId`, and `scan_events.checkpoint_id` is
`NOT NULL`. Folder `04` must have run. Everything else in this folder is self-contained.

item.name: 06 - Fleet & IoT Service

request.description:
Trucks. Enveloped `ApiResponse<PageResponse<VehicleResponse>>` - note this service uses the **dotted lower-case**
permission style (`fleet.vehicles.read`, `fleet.vehicles.create`, `fleet.vehicles.manage`) while organization, user
and tour services use UPPER_SNAKE. Both live in the same `permissions` table.

Also supports `sortBy` / `sortDir`, which the other list endpoints do not - the fleet service is the only one with a
server-side sort contract.

`CreateVehicleRequest` requires only `licensePlate`, and `vehicles.license_plate` is `VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE` - so the
plate must stay inside 20 characters. `LT-` plus the 15-character `{{uniq}}` is 18, deliberately under the limit.

`organizationId` is the owning transporter, not the marketer.

**This is a 201, not a 200** - `VehicleController.createVehicle` explicitly sets `HttpStatus.CREATED`, unlike most
other create endpoints in the platform. The test accepts both anyway so a future normalisation does not break it.

Single truck, enveloped. `certificateExpiryAt` is the compliance field: an expired certificate is what a CSPH
inspection actually checks, and the platform surfaces it here rather than only in a report.

Updates the truck''s specification and status. `status: MAINTENANCE` is the interesting part - a truck in the
workshop must not be assignable to a tour, and this is the request that would put it in that state before anyone
tries.

body.raw:
{
  "licensePlate": "LT-{{uniq}}",
  "type": "VRAC",
  "organizationId": "{{transporterOrgId}}",
  "maxVolume": 15.0,
  "maxBottleCount": 24,
  "certificateNumber": "CERT-{{uniq}}",
  "tareWeight": 4400.0,
  "isActive": true,
  "status": "MAINTENANCE",
  "statusDescription": "Sent to the workshop by the csph-gateway Postman collection"
}

request.description:
IoT devices - GPS trackers, PDA handhelds and RFID readers (`DeviceType`: `GPS`, `PDA`, `RFIDREADER`), each
optionally assigned to a person or a vehicle.

Filterable by `organizationId`, `deviceType`, `status`. Enveloped `PageResponse`, like `/vehicles` in the same
service.

`CreateDeviceRequest` requires `serialNumber` **and** `deviceType`; `devices.serial_number` is `VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE`,
so `{{uniq}}` is ample.

`deviceType` is the common `DeviceType` enum - `GPS`, `PDA` or `RFIDREADER` - not a free string, and the pairing of
`batteryLevel` with the derived `batteryCritical` flag is how a low-battery handheld gets flagged before it dies
mid-tour.

**201 Created**, like `POST /vehicles` and for the same reason.

Single device, enveloped. `lastLatitude` / `lastLongitude` / `lastSync` are the cached position - deliberately
separate from the telemetry history below, because a device that stopped reporting looks identical to a stationary
one unless you look at `lastSync`.

Firmware and health update. `batteryLevel: 22` with `batteryCritical: true` is the state that should raise an
operational alert - this is the request that would drive one, and the status is set to `LOW_BATTERY` to match.

`UpdateDeviceRequest` is the only update DTO in the platform that also accepts `lastSync`, `lastLatitude` and
`lastLongitude`, because device positions arrive out of band from the tracker rather than through the REST client.

Assigns the device to a driver **and** a truck in one call - which is the real-world pairing, since a handheld rides
in a specific truck with a specific person. `AssignDeviceRequest` has no `@NotBlank`, so assigning to nobody is a
legal (if useless) request.

Person and vehicle ids were captured in folder `03` (`personIdNew`) and this folder (`vehicleId`).

Releases the device back to the pool. **No request body at all** - the server nulls both assignment columns itself,
so sending `{"assignedToPersonId": null}` is unnecessary and would be ignored anyway.

Unassigning is what makes a device re-assignable: the platform treats a device with a stale assignment as in use,
which is how a handheld goes missing from the fleet view.

High-frequency GPS ingest from the tracker. `TelemetryIngestRequest` requires `vehicleId`, `latitude` and
`longitude`; everything else is optional.

**The response is 201 with a completely EMPTY body** - the handler returns `ResponseEntity.status(CREATED).build()`
with no payload at all. Calling `pm.response.json()` on it throws, so this request deliberately asserts on the status
only. This is the one place in the suite where a JSON assertion would be wrong.

In production this endpoint is the one that should be reachable by device credential rather than user JWT; the
`TELEMETRY_INGEST` permission annotation is the current stand-in for that.

The truck''s most recent known position.

**The response is a BARE object, not an `ApiResponse` envelope** - `ResponseEntity<TelemetryResponse>` rather than
`ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<TelemetryResponse>>`. The `TelemetryResponse` fields are at the top level, so
`j.data` does not exist. The test below reads the top-level keys.

This is the inconsistency that makes the telemetry controller the odd one out in the whole platform, and it is worth
knowing before writing a client against it: three adjacent endpoints, three different response conventions.

The trajectory between two instants - what a route replay or a geofence check consumes.

**Also bare: a bare JSON array**, not an envelope and not a `PageResponse`. Both `start` and `end` are optional and
ISO-8601 (`@DateTimeFormat(iso = DATE_TIME)`); omitting them returns everything stored, which on a long-lived
tracker is a lot of rows. The values here come from the collection pre-request (`periodStart` = 30 days ago,
`periodEnd` = now), so the window is wide enough to catch the telemetry point just ingested.

Unlike the single-position route, this one has **no** `@RequiresPermission`, so it answers without the permission
headers the gateway supplies.

**Last request in folder `06`** - removes the truck created near the top, after its device has been assigned,
unassigned and after telemetry has been ingested against it.

Note the asymmetry: the **device** created in this folder is not deleted. A device outlives the vehicle it was
mounted in, and the field history has to stay resolvable - which is also why `POST /telemetry` above needed a real
`vehicleId` rather than a random UUID.

item.description:
fleet-device-service on :8088, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1` - trucks (`/vehicles`), IoT devices
(`/devices`) and GPS telemetry (`/telemetry`).

**Three different response conventions in three adjacent controllers:** `/vehicles` and `/devices` are enveloped
`ApiResponse<PageResponse<...>>`, while `/telemetry` answers a bare object on ingest, a **bare object** for the
latest position, and a **bare array** for a trajectory. This is the folder where the bare-vs-envelope distinction
bites hardest.

**Creates here return 201**, unlike most of the platform''s create endpoints.

item.name: 07 - Subsidy Service

request.description:
Volume declarations - a marketer declares the volume it sold in a period, and that declaration is the starting point
of the subsidy chain. Enveloped `PageResponse`, filterable by `declaringOrganizationId`, `siteId`, `status`, `period`.

Lifecycle: `DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> RECONCILED -> DISPUTED` (`DeclarationStatus`). The whole folder below walks one
declaration through those transitions.

`CreateDeclarationRequest` requires `periodStart` and `periodEnd` (`@NotNull`); the organisation and site are
optional at this layer, and `getEffectiveOrganizationId()` falls back from `declaringOrganizationId` to
`marketerOrganizationId` - so sending both is the explicit, unambiguous choice.

`declaredVolume` is what the marketer *claims*. The whole point of the reconciliation below is to compare that claim
against the tracked volume, so a deliberate 1-unit overstatement here is what makes the redressement step
meaningful rather than a formality.

The period window comes from the collection pre-request, so it is always "the last 30 days" relative to the run.

Single declaration, enveloped. The natural place to watch `status` and `statusDate` as the folder walks the
lifecycle.

Editable only while the declaration is still a `DRAFT` - that is enforced in the service, so this request must run
**before** the `submit` step below. Amending a submitted declaration would defeat the audit trail the subsidy
process depends on.

`declaredVolume` is revised from 12.0 to 13.5, which widens the gap the reconciliation will find.

Hands the declaration to the regulator: `DRAFT -> SUBMITTED`. No body, no parameters.

Every subsequent action (review, approve, reject) is only legal from `SUBMITTED`, so folder order is load-bearing
here in a way it is not for a simple CRUD resource.

A CSPH agent reviews the declaration. Both query parameters are **optional** (`required = false`) - unlike
`assign-vehicle`, `skip`, `approve` and `approvedQuantity` elsewhere - but a review with no reviewer and no notes is
useless in practice, so both are supplied.

This is the human checkpoint between the marketer''s claim and the regulator''s decision.

The regulator approves the declared volume, which is what makes the volume subsidy-eligible. `approvedByPersonId`
and `notes` are optional query parameters.

`approve` is deliberately **not** followed by `reject`: rejecting an already-approved declaration is a state-machine
error, and the request below exists to demonstrate that the lifecycle is actually enforced.

Rejects the declaration, routing it to `DISPUTED`. Both query parameters are optional.

Because the request above already tried to approve it, this is **expected to be rejected** - and that is the point
of the test. A declaration that accepted both `approve` and `reject` would mean the state machine is not enforced,
which is a much more serious finding than a red test here.

Reconciliations - the regulator''s measured answer to the marketer''s claim. Enveloped `PageResponse`, filterable by
`declarationId` and `status` (`PENDING`, `VERIFIED`, `REDRESSEMENTAPPLIED`).

One reconciliation per declaration (`reconciliations.declaration_id` is `UNIQUE`), which is why the by-declaration
route below can 404 for a declaration that has not been reconciled yet.

`CreateReconciliationRequest` requires `declarationId` (`@NotBlank`) and nothing else - the tracked figures are all
optional.

The numbers tell the story: 13.5 t declared against 12.0 t tracked, i.e. a 1.5 t overstatement, and one more bottle
going out than coming back. `trackedBottlesOut - trackedBottlesIn` is the leak that the redressement amount below is
computed from; `subsidyRate` is the per-tonne rate the regulator applies to the gap.

body.raw:
{
  "declarationId": "{{declarationId}}",
  "trackedVolume": 12.0,
  "trackedBottlesOut": 14,
  "trackedBottlesIn": 13,
  "subsidyRate": 625.0,
  "verifiedByPersonId": "{{personId}}",
  "notes": "Postman reconciliation probe - 1.5 t less than declared"
}

request.description:
Single reconciliation, enveloped. This is the record a marketer disputes: declared vs tracked volume, bottle
imbalance, and the rate applied.

Reverse lookup: given a declaration, return its reconciliation. Because `declaration_id` is `UNIQUE` this can only
ever return one object, and it **404s** when the declaration has not been reconciled.

`/declaration/{declarationId}` (singular) - easy to mistype next to `/reconciliations/{id}`.

Signs off the reconciliation: `PENDING -> VERIFIED`. Both query parameters are optional.

Verification is the point of no return - it is what authorises the redressement below, so it is deliberately placed
before the `pay` / `cancel` pair.

Redressements - the financial penalty a marketer owes when tracked volume falls short of declared volume. The last
link in the chain: declaration -> reconciliation -> redressement -> payment.

Enveloped `PageResponse`, filterable by `reconciliationId` and `status`.

`CreateRedressementRequest` requires `reconciliationId` (`@NotBlank`) and `dueDate` (`@NotNull`); `amount` and
`transactionRef` are optional.

`amount` is hand-set to 937.5 - exactly 1.5 t of overstatement at the 625 per-tonne `subsidyRate` declared above.
Deriving it that way makes the number checkable by hand, which is the property that matters in a subsidy dispute.

`dueDate` comes from the collection pre-request (30 days out), so the penalty is never already overdue.
Single redressement, enveloped. `status` here is the whole story: `PENDING` until `pay` or `cancel` resolves it.

Records payment of the penalty. `transactionRef` is an **optional** query parameter, but a redressement marked paid
with no bank reference is unauditable, so one is always supplied - carrying `{{uniq}}` to keep re-runs distinct.

`{{uniq}}` is regenerated per request, so this reference differs from the one sent at creation. That is harmless: the
two are independent columns, and the payment reference is the authoritative one.

Cancels the penalty - used when the reconciliation itself is overturned on appeal. No body, no parameters.

Runs after `pay`, so cancelling a paid redressement is correctly refused. Same reasoning as the declaration
`reject` step: a resource that accepted both would mean the state machine is decorative.

item.description:
subsidy-service on :8089, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1` - the financial core: volume declarations, their
reconciliation against tracked movements, and the redressements that follow a shortfall.

**The chain is strictly ordered** - declaration -> reconciliation -> redressement - and each link only accepts its
own predecessor''s identifier. A reconciliation cannot exist before its declaration, and a redressement cannot exist
before its reconciliation.

**Deliberate state-machine rejections.** Four requests in this folder (`reject` after `approve`, `cancel` after
`pay`, and the two conflicting pickup / tour transitions in folder `04`) are *expected* to be refused. Those tests
assert `200|409|422` and log the body. A pass there means the lifecycle is enforced; a failure would mean it is not.

item.name: 08 - Audit Service

request.description:
Field-level change history. Enveloped `ApiResponse<PageResponse<EntityModificationResponse>>` - enveloped, unlike the
bare lists elsewhere.

`entityType` and `entityId` are optional filters, bound through an `AuditQueryParams` `@ModelAttribute`; `page` and
`size` default to `0` / `20`. `actorPersonId`, `action`, `module`, `dateFrom` and `dateTo` are also available and
simply not exercised here.

A row here is one entity modification, whose nested `changes` list is the individual before/after field pairs - the
granularity a GPL audit actually requires.

The status-change journal - who moved which entity from which status to which, and when. Enveloped `PageResponse`.

Same `AuditQueryParams` binding as `/modifications`, so the same filters apply. Kept separate from `/modifications`
because status transitions are the queries regulators ask for by name, and they are indexed differently.

Per-entity audit summary - counts by action and by actor for one entity.

**The path has two variable segments** (`{entityType}/{entityId}`), and `entityType` is the **entity''s** type, not
the API module: `ORGANIZATION`, `SITE`, `PERSON`, `CYLINDER`, `RFID_TAG`, `TOUR`, `VEHICLE`, `DECLARATION` ... The
module (`AUTH`, `TOUR`, `FLEET`) is a different concept and a different field, which is an easy and silent
mistake - a wrong `entityType` returns 404, not an empty summary.

**The body is a RAW `AuditEvent`, not wrapped in an `ApiResponse` envelope** - this is the one write endpoint in the
platform that takes a bare domain object. (Responses are enveloped as usual.)

`AuditEvent` is the message every microservice publishes on the broker after a write, and audit-service consumes it
into `EntityModification` + `FieldChange` rows. This endpoint is the synchronous equivalent - useful for replaying
events, and for testing the ingestion path without a broker.

The field is `actionDescription`; note that `AuthService` sends `description` instead, and both exist on the DTO -
another small inconsistency in the same audit surface. Both are sent here so the event is complete either way.

body.raw:
{
  "entityType": "ORGANIZATION",
  "entityId": "{{orgId}}",
  "entityName": "Postman Test Org {{uniq}}",
  "action": "UPDATE",
  "actionDescription": "Postman suite ingest probe",
  "description": "Emitted by the csph-gateway Postman collection",
  "module": "ORGANIZATION",
  "changeby": "{{personId}}",
  "changedate": "{{nowIso}}",
  "changes": [
    { "fieldName": "status", "fieldLabel": "Statut", "oldValue": "INACTIVE", "newValue": "ACTIVE", "valueType": "STRING" }
  ],
  "deviceInfo": "Postman",
  "ipAddress": "127.0.0.1"
}

item.description:
audit-service on :8084, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1`.

Read side: `/modifications` (field-level), `/status-history` (status transitions), `/summary/{entityType}/{entityId}`

item.name: 09 - Notification Service

request.description:
`CreateTemplateRequest` marks **every** field `@NotBlank` - code, name, subject, bodyTemplate, module, channel,
language. That is the strictest create DTO in the platform, and the 400 message names the offending field.

`code` is the business key used by `/notifications/send` and by `/{code}` lookups, so it carries `{{uniq}}`.

`bodyTemplate` uses `{{placeholder}}` syntax (double braces) resolved at send time by
`NotificationService.resolvePlaceholders` against the request's `variables` map. An unresolved placeholder is left
in the body verbatim - there is no error, which is worth remembering when a notification arrives with literal
`{{reference}}` in it.

**The body sends `\{\{recipientName\}\}` with escaped braces, and that matters.** Postman substitutes `{{...}}` in
request bodies before the request is sent, so an unescaped placeholder would be replaced with an empty string and
the stored template would lose its slots. `\{\{` is how you send a literal `{{`.

`channel` is `EMAIL` here. Changing it later changes whether the send actually attempts SMTP.

body.raw:
{
  "code": "PM-TPL-{{uniq}}",
  "name": "Postman Template {{uniq}}",
  "subject": "Notification Postman {{uniq}}",
  "bodyTemplate": "Bonjour \{\{recipientName\}\}, votre demande \{\{reference\}\} est \{\{status\}\}. Merci de confirmer la reception. - Postman probe",
  "module": "TOUR",
  "channel": "EMAIL",
  "language": "FR"
}

request.description:
The whole template catalogue. Enveloped **array** (not a `PageResponse` - the catalogue is small and never paged).

`language` is part of the template, so a French and an English variant are two distinct rows with two distinct
codes; the catalogue is therefore the place to check whether a translation actually exists before debugging a
"notification in the wrong language" report.

Single template, addressed by **code** - the business key, not a UUID. `{{templateCode}}` is captured by the create
request above, and this route has no `/{id}` variant, so a UUID here is a guaranteed 404.

Sends a notification built from a template.

**`recipientEmail` is deliberately NOT sent.** It is optional, and when it is absent `NotificationService` logs
`Channel EMAIL not supported or missing email for ...` and skips the SMTP call entirely - the notification is still
recorded, and the endpoint still answers **200**. That keeps this request working against a local MailHog (or with
no SMTP server at all), which is what you want from a repeatable suite.

If you do add `recipientEmail`, the send attempts real SMTP against `spring.mail.host`
(`MAIL_HOST`, default `smtp.gmail.com:587`). Any failure is caught and recorded as `status: FAILED` on the log row -
the endpoint still answers 200. Check `{{mailhogWeb}}` (MailHog UI, default :8026) for captured mail.

The response is an `ApiResponse<NotificationResponse>` carrying the log row''s `id`, `status` and `sentAt`.

item.description:
notification-service on :8085, reached through `{{gateway}}/api/v1` - templates (`/notification-templates`) and
sending (`/notifications/send`).

Templates are addressed by **business `code`**, never by UUID - there is no `/{id}` route.

`POST /notifications/send` omits `recipientEmail` on purpose so no SMTP connection is attempted and the endpoint
answers a clean 200. See the request description for what changes if you add it, and where to look afterwards
(`{{mailhogWeb}}`).
